facts.text: I do not accept that the definition of building works includes the rectification of defects in the building works notified during the defects liability period.
The contract defines building works as works that are carried out, completed and handed over to the owner.

The contract defines practical completion as when building works are complete except for minor omissions and defects that do not prevent the building works from being reasonably capable of being used for their usual purpose.
The contract states that the defects liability period commences on and including the date of practical completion.
The contract states that before the end of the defects liability period the owner may give the builder one list of defects in the building works that appear after the date of practical completion.

Section 48K(7) stated that the Tribunal does not have jurisdiction in respect of a building claim arising from a breach of a statutory warranty implied under Part 2C if the date on which the claim was lodged is more than 7 years after the date the residential building work was completed.

Section 48K(7) also stated that if the work is not completed, the relevant date is the date for completion specified or determined in accordance with the contract, or if there is no such date, the date of the contract.
Section 3B was introduced by the Home Building Amendment Act 2011.
The amendments enacted by the Home Building Amendment Act 2011 were made for the purpose of the avoidance of doubt.
The amendments enacted by the Home Building Amendment Act 2011, including section 3B, extend to residential building work commenced or completed before 1 February 2012.
The contract in this case was entered into in 2009.
The completion of residential building work occurs on the date that the work is complete within the meaning of the contract under which the work was done.
If the contract does not provide for when work is complete (or there is no contract), the completion of residential building work occurs on practical completion of the work.

The completion of residential building work is practical completion when the work is completed except for any omissions or defects that do not prevent the work from being reasonably capable of being used for its intended purpose.

I took the position that practical completion of residential building work occurred on the earliest of the contractor handing over possession, the contractor last attending the site to carry out work (excluding defect remedy work not affecting practical completion), the issue of an occupation certificate authorising use or occupation, or (for owner-builder work) 18 months after the issue of the owner-builder permit.
I concluded that the statutory warranty period commenced on completion of the building works within the meaning of the contract, meaning when the works reached practical completion.
It is not in dispute that the owners took possession of the works on 13 July 2017.
I concluded that issue of the FOC is not the completion date of the works under section 3B.
I concluded that the Tribunal erred in finding that the date of completion of the building works was 20 October 2010 when the FOC was issued.
I concluded that the Tribunal misinterpreted the contract and did not correctly apply sections 48K(7) and 3B of the HB Act.
I concluded that ground 6 is established.
I concluded that if the completion date was not the date of practical completion (8 July 2010), it was the date on which the works were handed over to the owners (13 July 2021).
I concluded that the Tribunal’s finding concerning the completion date gives rise to an injustice to the builder which is reasonably clear.
I concluded that the parties did not enter into a new contract or vary their original contract.
I concluded that the respondent’s application to the Tribunal was out of time because the owners’ proceedings were not commenced within seven years of completion of the building works.
The Tribunal has no power to extend time for the making of an application under the HB Act.
I concluded that the appropriate orders are that the appeal be allowed, the decision under appeal be set aside, and the Tribunal proceedings be dismissed.
The Tribunal formed a provisional view that the builder should be ordered to pay the owners’ costs.
The case S & G Homes Pty Ltd t/as Pavilion Homes v Owen [2015] NSWCATAP 190 at [53] was cited regarding the Tribunal’s power to extend time.

keyphrases: issue of FOC not completion date
Tribunal no power to extend time

events.text: Owners took possession of the works
Tribunal finding that completion date was 20 October 2010 (FOC issued)
Practical completion date referenced as 8 July 2010
Works handed over to the owners (as an alternative completion date)
